source_title: Copilot skills for building feedback loops, delegating safely, and moving repeatable work into automations. - GitHub
source_excerpt:
Feedback loops for coding agents. A Copilot plugin.
In the Copilot app, open these links. Each one asks you to confirm, then opens a pre-filled form:
Or do it by hand: Customize → + Add → Marketplace with github/lever , then + Add → Plugin with lever@lever .
Start a new session and try one that only reads:
You get a Loop Card back: the metric, how to measure it, how noisy it is, and what counts as a win. Nothing gets pushed, filed or merged.
Agents get really good once they can check their own work. Give one a number, a way to measure it and a bar for "better", and it'll grind on that for hours without you. Without that, you're the loop: pasting screenshots, eyeballing scroll jank, hitting rerun on CI at midnight.
Setting up the loop is the hard part. What do you measure? How noisy is it? What's a real win and what's a lucky run? When do you stop? Most people skip it, which is fair, because it's annoying. lever asks you those questions, writes the answers down, and then lets agents iterate against it.
It comes from how some of the most AI-forward engineers at GitHub work day to day: CI speedups, a five-day crate split run from three terminals, weeks of unattended delivery , and the automations that took over the chores. We mined our own sessions for what kept working, then put most of the effort into making it one command. Same workflow, no PhD required.
More in the examples gallery : experiment arms, a brief, the three-terminal refactor, the PR shepherd, cross-model review, an automation, and the verbs that tune lever to you.
Each verb is a skill in skills/ . The / menu shows only /lever . Skills that only read and advise, like loop , can still load on their own when your ask fits. Anything that pushes, files, opens PRs or schedules runs waits for /lever or an explicit ask.
Autonomy , L0 to L5: who merges. L0 only proposes. L2 gets PRs green and you merge. L5 lands, releases and watches. It's your setting, saved in ~/.copilot/lever.yml , and your repo's branch protection still wins. Start at L2 and turn it up as you trust it.
Spend , standard · high · max : model tier, parallel lanes, review depth and how often things run. A repo can cap it in .github/lever.yml .
/lever setup asks three questions and writes both ( example ). For a team, copy config/autonomy.example.yml to .github/lever.yml .
Work lever starts is tracked as an issue assigned to you with the lever label , so /lever status can list everything in flight, needs-you first.
Per repo , so the Copilot coding agent in the cloud gets the skills too:
Skills link to ../../docs/... , so those four folders have to sit next to skills/ .
Hacking on lever: clone it and run copilot plugin marketplace add ./lever , then copilot plugin install lever@lever . It loads straight from your checkout, so edits show up in your next session.
Automations: the recipes in automations/ install through the GitHub MCP server with /lever automate . Each one starts paused, dry-runs on past events, and only then gets turned on. The Copilot app has the automation tools built in; in Copilot CLI, start with copilot --enable-all-github-mcp-tools .
These skills fit how we work. Yours will be different. /lever mirror reads your own session history and shows you what you keep repeating, and /lever steer turns those repeated corrections into rules that stick. Fork it and bend it.
Copilot skills for building feedback loops, delegating safely, and moving repeatable work into automations.
